Section-by-section breakdown · 20 Aug 2026

Eight sections,
taken apart.

Reference: vita-travel.webflow.io, by Phenomenon Studio. Yours: TripMate's landing on feat/ui-optimization. Every number here was read from live computed styles or quoted from source — nothing is eyeballed from a screenshot.

You are much closer than the last audit suggests. The gap left is not polish — it is one typeface instead of three, headings roughly twice the size, a repeating section opener, and a veil over your photographs that should not be there.

00 / Correction

Most of the old
audit is done

design-audit.html was written on 19 August. Six of its recommendations have since shipped, and one of its defects was never a defect. Read this table before acting on anything in that file.

The audit saidVerified in source today
Root font-size"16px fixed" — called the single biggest winDone. globals.css:12 is clamp(16px, 1.13vw, 20px)
TypefacesFive, including Playfair DisplayThree. Playfair is fully removed — layout.tsx:2 loads Archivo, Source Serif 4, Manrope
Containermax-w-6xl, a 1152px boxGone. No max-width anywhere on the landing; sections are full-bleed px-5 sm:px-6
Corner radius16/12/4px on nearly everythingDone for the photo cards — ImageRow.tsx:99 has no radius, and a comment saying why
Image ratio"no ratio discipline"Done. aspect-[11/12] = 0.917, against Vita's measured 0.915
Card meta"title over caption, no rule, no meta"Done. ImageRow.tsx:91 is title-left / stat-right on a border-b border-white/10
Motion"the landing fades; nothing is split, pinned or scrubbed"Done. useLineReveal runs SplitText masked line reveals on the Hero h1 and HowItWorks h2; ScrollTrigger drives ImageRow and HeroPoster

And one diagnosis to throw away

The audit says the Blue Hour photos are "visibly soft — replace the sources, yours are upscaled or over-compressed." The source files are fine. Every photo has a backdrop-filter: blur(3px) saturate(110%) painted over it by .scene-frost (globals.css:1116), which only clears on hover. Buying new photographs would have changed nothing.

The blur is deliberate — the source comment records that 7px "hid the subject entirely and made the row look like it had failed to load", so it was tuned down to 3px. It is a considered decision, not a bug. It is also the single biggest visual difference between your card row and theirs, and it is invisible on touch, where the veil is disabled entirely.

01 / System

Their whole system,
on one screen

Root font-size is 1.11vw — 12.57px at 1131px wide. Every value below is in rem, so the page zooms as one drawing instead of reflowing. That single decision is why it survives a 27-inch monitor.

The type ramp, rendered at its real sizes

Travel11.87rem · 600 · lh 1.00 · −0.067em  (shown at 3.75rem)
Section heading3.75rem · 600 · lh 1.10 · −0.076em
100+2.81rem · 600 · lh 1.00 · −0.085em
7 Day Mystic Mountain1.75rem · 600 · lh 1.20 · −0.091em

Explore0.87rem · 600 · lh 0.90 · −0.045em

The signature: tracking tightens as the type shrinks. −0.067em at the hero, −0.106em at 1.5rem. That is backwards from normal typographic practice, where small text is loosened for legibility. It is also why every line reads as one packed shape. Nothing on their page is at zero or positive.

02 / Sections

Eight sections,
eight jobs

Each one below: what it looks like, what it is made of, the single rule it teaches, and what you have in its place.

Section 01

Intro — one word, full bleed

Vita · .intro · 1440×922

TripMate · Hero.tsx · 1440×900

Anatomy

photo, full bleed, no overlay scrim
  "Travel"        11.87rem / 600 / −0.067em
  support         1.12rem, two lines, centred
  pill CTA        white fill, radius 5rem

The rule it teaches

One word can carry a viewport. The headline is not a sentence — it is a shape. All the meaning is delegated to the two lines beneath it, set eleven times smaller.

Yours

A full sentence — "Somewhere, it's the blue hour." — in italic Source Serif 4 at clamp(2.25rem, 6.5vw, 5rem). Deliberately CTA-free, which is a real and defensible choice. But at 5rem against their 11.87rem it is less than half the size, and a wrapping serif sentence reads as a caption where theirs reads as a poster.

Section 02

Statistic — the ruled card grid

Vita · .statistic-section · three cards, zero gap, vertical hairlines between

Anatomy

grid 3 × 1fr, gap 0
  ├ hairline between cells (not around them)
  ├ head:  title left · "/ 78+ Countries" right
  ├ rule:  1px white-10%
  └ img:   0.915 portrait, radius 0, cover

The rule it teaches

Share one rule; do not give each card a box. Zero gap plus a single dividing hairline reads as one ruled grid. A gap plus a border per card reads as four separate stickers.

Yours — closer than anything else on the page

ImageRow.tsx:91 already does title-left / stat-right on a border-b border-white/10, at aspect-[11/12] with no radius. Two things differ: you use gap-4 md:gap-6 with a border on each card rather than a shared rule and no gap — and the leading slash is missing from the meta, which is a surprising amount of what makes theirs read as editorial.

Section 04

Featured — the dense card

Vita · .featured-section · 1440×1496 — the longest section on the page

Anatomy

header:  heading left · support copy right
grid 2 × 2, gap 0, hairlines both axes
card = grid[1fr 1fr], gap 2.5rem
  ├ title    1.75rem / 600 / −0.091em
  ├ price    "from $1,000", $ emphasised
  ├ 4 spec rows, tiny icon right-aligned
  ├ rating   5 stars, #fb9826
  └ CTA      dark pill + glyph
image right, 0.915 portrait, radius 0

The rule it teaches

State the facts permanently. Price, location, dates, duration, guest count and social proof are all visible without interaction. The card is dense because density is what makes a listing feel real.

Also note the header: heading left, support paragraph right. It is a section opener with the second column used for prose instead of content.

Yours

You have no equivalent. The nearest is the Blue Hour row, whose detail line (.scene-card-detail) is opacity: 0 until hover — so on a phone, in a screenshot, and for anyone who does not hover, those facts do not exist.

Section 05

Combine — numbered steps over a photograph

Vita · .combine-section · a five-column strip laid over full-bleed imagery

Anatomy

full-bleed photo, darkened
strip: 5 columns, vertical hairlines
  col 1  copy, 1rem
  cols 2-5:
    "01"     2.81rem / 600 / −0.085em
    "Step"   0.62rem, white-50
    label    pushed to the cell's bottom

The rule it teaches

Put the process on top of the atmosphere. One element does two jobs — the photograph keeps the page cinematic while the strip does the explaining, so the section costs no extra scroll.

Yours

HowItWorks.tsx is the same content — three numbered steps — but on a flat gradient band with no imagery, and the numbers are text-3xl italic serif at text-muted/60. Theirs are 2.81rem grotesk. Compare the two screenshots below.

Vita · .how-works-section

TripMate · HowItWorks.tsx — the heading wraps to three lines in a 14rem column

Section 06

Destination — the accent's one appearance

Vita · .destination-section · the only place #fb9826 does real work

The rule: spend the accent once, on the thing you most want looked at. Everything else on their page is white at some alpha. Yours: amber appears on the CTA, in .hero-light's ambient glow and in .scene-void's radial — more present than theirs, though all three are defensible. You already have a globe that could do exactly this job.

Sections 08 – 09

People, then a real footer

Vita · names set inside the image, bottom-left, no rule

Vita · +Coaches / +Contacts at 2.81rem

The rule: the footer is a section, not a legal strip. Navigation is set at 2.81rem — larger than most sites' headings — with a white-40 + prefix, over a hairline, above a small bar carrying copyright and legal. Yours: the landing has no footer at all. It ends on the poster CTA.

03 / Components

Rebuilt, side
by side

Not screenshots — these are live, built from the measured values. Resize the window and both sides scale together. The markup is copy-pasteable.

The section opener

Vita

❋  About Us

Not just trips experiences that nurture body and soul

TripMate

How it actually works.

Left column empty, heading roughly a third the size, no label, no rule. The offset grid already exists in HowItWorks.tsx:56 as lg:grid-cols-[14rem_1fr] — the column is simply unoccupied.

The pattern, verbatim

<div class="grid gap-10 border-t border-white/10 pt-10 lg:grid-cols-[11rem_1fr] lg:gap-10">
  <p class="flex items-center gap-2 text-sm font-semibold leading-none
            tracking-[-.045em] text-white/40">
    <span class="text-accent">❋</span> Journey
  </p>
  <h2 class="text-[3.75rem] font-semibold leading-[1.05] tracking-[-.076em]">
    How it actually works
  </h2>
</div>

This contradicts DESIGN.md's No-Kicker Rule — "Nothing sits above a headline. No eyebrows, no all-caps kickers, no category labels introducing a title." You have authorised trying it. If it ships, amend that rule in DESIGN.md with the reason rather than leaving a law the code breaks.

The card head

Vita
Introvert Retreats / 78+ Countries
TripMate
The Blue Hour One 20-minute window

Structurally the same — you got here already. What differs: their label is 1.12rem/600 against your 0.875rem/500, their tracking is −0.035em against your −0.01em, their meta leads with a slash, and the right-hand panel carries the real .scene-frost veil so you can see what it does to a photograph at rest.

The button

Vita
Explore Retreats ◼

radius 5rem · pad 1.25/2rem · white fill · no border · 0.875rem/600

TripMate
Plan a trip

radius full · px-8 py-4 · amber fill · shadow-lg · 1rem/500

Near-identical geometry. Three differences: they set the label smaller and heavier (0.875rem/600 vs your 1rem/500), they track it in at −0.045em, and they carry a trailing glyph. Yours adds a drop shadow — documented and deliberate, because it is the one button that sits on bare terrain.

04 / Gaps

What is
actually left

Ranked by how much each changes the first impression, per unit of work.

01

Take the veil off the photographs

.scene-frost blurs all four Blue Hour photos at rest and clears only on hover. At 2× it does not read as "slightly soft" — the subjects are unrecognisable. It is also disabled entirely under @media (hover: none), so phone users already see the version you would be shipping.

Fix

Drop the resting blur; keep the hover transition for the detail
overlay. One line in globals.css:1116.

02

Double the section headings

HowItWorks is text-3xl sm:text-4xl — 1.875 to 2.25rem, against Vita's 3.75rem. The distance between body and heading is where the drama lives, and at present there is barely any. This costs one class.

03

Add the section opener

Label pinned left, heading offset right, hairline above. Their most recognisable move, and the grid is already in your markup. Authorised — amend the No-Kicker Rule when it ships.

04

Cut to one display face, and stop stretching it

Archivo 900 for the poster and Source Serif 4 italic for scene headings are two display faces doing one job. Worse, .font-scene-hero carries font-stretch: 125% — widening a heavy grotesk is the strongest template tell there is, and Vita never touches the width axis.

Fix

font-stretch: normal;  letter-spacing: -.075em;

Then pick ONE of Archivo / Source Serif 4 for all display type.
Keeping the serif is the more distinctive choice — it is the one
thing you have that Vita does not.

05

Unhide the card facts

.scene-card-detail is opacity: 0 until hover. Vita states price, dates, guests and rating permanently. Facts a visitor must discover are facts most visitors never see.

06

Share one rule instead of four borders

gap-4 md:gap-6 plus border border-card-border per card gives four floating tiles. Zero gap plus one dividing hairline gives a ruled grid. Same tokens, different reading.

07

End the page

There is no footer. The landing stops on the poster CTA, which leaves the visitor with nowhere to go but back. Their footer is a full section with 2.81rem navigation.

05 / Missing

The sections
you don't have

Vita runs to ~6.9 screens against your ~3.1. Length is not the goal — but each of these earns its scroll. The real cost is content and imagery, not code, so they are listed with what each would need from you.

What it doesWhat you'd have to supply
Proof bandThree ruled cards, a number and a portrait eachThree true numbers. Trips planned, destinations covered, average plan cost — you have all three in the database
About splitTwo columns: imagery left, the argument right~60 words on why an itinerary that prices itself matters. No new photography needed
Featured plans2×2 dense cards: price, dates, duration, rating, CTAThe highest-value addition. You generate real itineraries — show four, with their real costs and dates. No stock imagery required
Process stripNumbered steps over full-bleed photographyNothing new. It is HowItWorks's existing copy moved onto one of the five photos in public/scenes/
Destination mapDark world map, accent dotsNothing new — you already ship a Cesium globe. This is the one section where you can beat them outright
FooterLarge navigation, contact, legal barLinks you already have in the navbar

Two of the six need no new assets at all, and the two strongest — featured plans and the destination map — are things you can build from data and code you already own. That is a better position than Vita's, which had to art-direct a photoshoot.

06 / Order

Do it in
this order

First — an hour

Drop the resting blur on the photos. Double the section headings. font-stretch: normal and −0.075em on the poster. Three edits, and they are the three you will notice most.

Then — the system

Section openers on all four beats, with DESIGN.md amended. One display face. Zero gap and a shared hairline on the card row. Unhide the card detail.

Then — the length

Featured plans from real generated itineraries. The globe as the destination section. A real footer. Only now is it worth adding scroll.

The last audit told you to delete variety until one system was left. You did most of it. What remains is not subtraction any more — it is amplification: the same system, set larger, labelled, and with nothing standing between the visitor and the photographs.
